course.description: Bring points together, trace a tangent and build an area. Discover how change accumulates.

lessons.title: What happens near the gap?

steps.headline: A limit is the value the outputs head towards as the input closes in on a point.

lead.text: Take h(x) = 10 − x and let x creep up on 4. At 4.1 the output is 5.9, at 4.01 it is 5.99, at 4.001 it is 5.999.
The outputs head towards 6, so 6 is the limit of h(x) as x approaches 4. A limit is about the nearby values, not about x = 4 itself.
Now try f(x) = x + 3. Let x get close to 2 from the left and from the right, and watch where the outputs go.

reveal.text: You followed the outputs from both sides and they met at 5. That meeting point is the limit.

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2.

workedSteps.text: Putting in x = 2 gives 0/0, which settles nothing.
Factor the top as a difference of squares.
Cancel x − 2. Near 2 it is never zero.
Let x approach 2.

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.

workedSteps.text: Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3).
Cancel x − 3, which is allowed because x is never 3 nearby.
Let x approach 3.

lead.text: Here the value at x = 2 has been set by hand. The graph on either side of it is a straight line.

reveal.text: Moving one point did not move the line around it. A limit follows the neighbours, not the value assigned at the point.

lead.text: Same shape, new numbers: a quotient that gives 0/0 at x = 4.

reveal.text: You cancelled the factor that caused the 0/0, then let x approach 4. The limit exists even though the quotient is undefined at 4.

lessons.orientation: Separate the value approached near a point from the value assigned at the point.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The quotient (x² − 9)/(x − 3) cannot take x = 3, because the bottom would be 0. But 3.1 is allowed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a limit by cancelling a common factor, and say why the value at the point does not matter.
intro.whyItMatters: Every derivative is a limit of this shape, where the quotient is undefined at the point.

recap.keyIdea: A limit is where the outputs head as the input closes in. It ignores the value at the point itself, so a 0/0 gap is settled by simplifying nearby.

blocks.text: You found that (x² − 9)/(x − 3) is 6.1 at x = 3.1, and that its limit at 3 is 6. You also saw that a value assigned at a hole does not move the limit.

recap.nextHook: Sometimes the two sides do not agree. What then?

lessons.title: Do both sides meet?

steps.headline: A limit can be taken from one side only.

lead.text: Your basket creeping up to £20 was a one-sided approach: the fee heads for £3. That is the left-hand limit at £20.
Coming down from above, the fee is £7. That is the right-hand limit.
Left means inputs smaller than the point. Right means inputs larger.
A function equals 2 for x < 0 and 5 for x ≥ 0. Follow its graph in towards 0 from the left.

reveal.text: Coming from the left you stayed on one level. What the function does at 0 itself, or on the right, does not change it.

lead.text: Same function. This time follow the graph in towards 0 from the right.

reveal.text: Left and right gave different numbers. The graph jumps at 0, so the two sides do not meet.

steps.headline: A function is continuous at a point when its limit there exists and equals its value.

lead.text: A two-sided limit exists only when the left-hand and right-hand limits agree. If they differ, it does not exist.
Continuous at a point needs three things: a value there, a two-sided limit there, and the two equal.

steps.headline: Is f continuous at 2, where f(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 7?

workedSteps.text: From the left, x + 2 heads for 4. From the right, it also heads for 4.
The sides agree, so the two-sided limit is 4.
Compare with the value at the point.
The limit and the value differ, so f is not continuous at 2.

lead.text: Another function, the same three questions. Look at the graph, then decide.

reveal.text: Each condition has to hold. Here the limit existed and the value existed, but they were not the same number.

lead.text: A graph has one missing point at x = 2. The line 2x + 4 runs through everything around it. You choose what goes in the gap.

reveal.text: Your value had to match what the neighbours head for: 2 × 2 + 4. That is how a single missing point is repaired.

lessons.orientation: Use one-sided limits and the value at the point to decide continuity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A shop charges £3 delivery on orders under £20 and £7 on orders of £20 or more.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell when a limit exists from both sides, and check whether a function is continuous at a point.
intro.whyItMatters: Continuity is the condition behind the derivative and the integral: both assume the graph has no jump.

recap.keyIdea: A two-sided limit exists only when both sides agree. A function is continuous where that limit exists and equals the value.

blocks.text: You read a left-hand limit of 2 and a right-hand limit of 5 for the same function, so it has no two-sided limit at 0. You also repaired a gap with the value 8.

recap.nextHook: Zoom in on a curve until the two sides agree on a slope.

lessons.title: Zoom in on a rate

steps.headline: The slope of a secant is the average rate over an interval.

lead.text: The odometer gave change in distance over change in time. For a curve, join two of its points with a line: that line is a secant.
Its slope is the average rate from a to b. For f(x) = x² from 0 to 2 it is (4 − 0)/2 = 2.
Take f(x) = x² between x = 1 and x = 3. Look at the secant joining those two points.

reveal.text: You divided the change in height by the change in input. That is the slope of the secant, and it belongs to the whole interval.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 1 to x = 1 + h, as h approaches 0.

workedSteps.text: Write the secant slope.
Expand the top.
Divide by h. Allowed, because h is never zero.
Let h approach 0.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 2 to x = 2 + h, as h approaches 0.

workedSteps.text: Expand the top.
Divide by h, for h ≠ 0.
Let h approach 0.

steps.headline: The derivative at a point is the limit of the secant slopes as the interval shrinks.

lead.text: As h shrinks, the secant swings round into the tangent. Its limiting slope is the derivative f′(a), the instantaneous rate at a.
A derivative is a slope, so it carries a sign: positive rising, negative falling.
Same method, a different point: x = 5. The secant slope has already been simplified.

reveal.text: The same move again: let the h term vanish and keep what is left. That limit is the derivative at 5.

lead.text: From x = 3 to x = 4 the secant slope of x² is 7. That averages the whole interval, so the rate right at 3 can differ.

reveal.text: At x = 3 the instantaneous rate is smaller than the average over the next unit, because the curve is still steepening.

lessons.orientation: Turn average rates over an interval into a derivative at a point.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A car's odometer reads 40 km at 1:00 and 100 km at 2:30.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn secant slopes into a derivative, and read it as the rate at one point.
intro.whyItMatters: Speed, growth and slope at an instant are all derivatives.

recap.keyIdea: The derivative at a point is the limit of the secant slopes as the interval shrinks: the rate at that instant.

blocks.text: You found an average rate of 4 for x² between 1 and 3, then watched the slope tend to 2 at x = 1 and to 4 at x = 2.

recap.nextHook: Computing every slope as a limit is slow. Is there a shortcut?

lessons.title: A rule for every power

steps.headline: To differentiate xⁿ, bring the power down and take one off it.

lead.text: Your pattern for x² was 2x: the power 2 came down and the power dropped to 1. The same move works for any power.
So x⁴ has derivative 4x³, and x⁵ has derivative 5x⁴.

steps.headline: Find f′(2) for f(x) = x⁴.

workedSteps.text: Bring the power down and take one off it.
Substitute x = 2.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same two moves: differentiate, then substitute. This time the function is a cube.

reveal.text: You brought the power down, dropped it by one, then substituted. That is the whole power rule.

steps.headline: Constants vanish, multiples stay, and sums are differentiated term by term.

lead.text: A constant only lifts the graph, so its slope is 0. A multiple stays in front: the derivative of 5x² is 5 × 2x. A sum is differentiated one term at a time.

steps.headline: Find g′(1) for g(x) = 2x² + 5.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate 2x²: keep the 2, bring down the power.
Differentiate 5: a constant.
Add the parts, then substitute x = 1.

lead.text: Apply the power rule to each term and add the results. Constants contribute nothing.

reveal.text: Each term gave its own piece: 6x from the square, −2 from the line, and 0 from the constant.

lead.text: The height 4 − x² peaks at x = 0. On the left it rises; on the right it falls.

reveal.text: f′(x) = −2x, so the slope at 1 is negative: the curve is falling. A negative rate does not mean the height is negative.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate polynomial terms and distinguish a derivative from a function value.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of the curve y = x².

intro.promise: By the end you'll differentiate any polynomial term by term, and read the sign of the result.
intro.whyItMatters: Differentiating polynomials by rule replaces every limit calculation from the last lesson.

recap.keyIdea: Bring the power down and take one off it, term by term; constants vanish and multiples stay.

blocks.text: You differentiated x⁴ to 4x³ and found a slope of 32 at 2. You also found that 4 − x² has slope −2 at 1.

recap.nextHook: What if the power is itself a function of x? The rule needs one more move.

lessons.title: A function inside a function

steps.headline: When one quantity sits inside another, their rates multiply.

lead.text: The bike had two stages. So does f(x) = (4x + 5)². The inner function u = 4x + 5 changes at rate 4. The outer function u² changes at rate 2u.
This is the chain rule: the outer rate at the inner value, times the inner rate.

steps.headline: Find f′(1) for f(x) = (4x − 3)².

workedSteps.text: Name the inner function. At x = 1 it equals 1.
The outer function, u², changes at rate 2u.
The inner function changes at 4 per unit of x.
Multiply the two rates.

lead.text: Same moves: name the inner function, find both rates, multiply. This time the inside is 2x + 1.

reveal.text: You took the outer rate at the inner value, then multiplied by how fast the inside moves. Without that second factor the answer would be too small.

steps.headline: Find f′(1) for f(x) = (3 − x)².

workedSteps.text: Inner function and its rate.
Outer rate.
Multiply by the inner rate, then put in x = 1.

lead.text: Say the rates out loud: the outer rate at the inside, then the inner rate.

reveal.text: The 6 is 2 × 3: twice the inner value's rate factor, kept next to the inner expression 3x + 1.

lead.text: A cube this time. You can check any answer by expanding (x + 2)³ and differentiating term by term: the two routes must agree.

reveal.text: Expanding gives x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8, whose derivative at 1 agrees with the chain rule. Two routes, one number.

lessons.orientation: Multiply outer and inner rates when differentiating a composition.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Your pedals make 1 turn each second. The wheel makes 3 turns for every pedal turn, and each wheel turn carries the bike 2 metres.

intro.promise: By the end you'll differentiate a function inside a function by multiplying the outer rate by the inner rate.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every real formula is a function inside a function.

recap.keyIdea: Rates in a chain multiply: differentiate the outer function at the inner value, then multiply by the inner function's rate.

blocks.text: You found that the bike covers 6 metres each second by multiplying 1 × 3 × 2. You used the same multiplication to get 8 for (4x − 3)² at x = 1.

recap.nextHook: Derivatives measure motion. Next: position, velocity and acceleration.

lessons.title: Read motion from a curve

steps.headline: Velocity is the derivative of position. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

lead.text: The lift's steady rate was the slope of its position graph. That slope at an instant is the velocity.
For s(t) = 4t² metres, v(t) = 8t m/s and a(t) = 8 m/s².

steps.headline: For s(t) = 3t² − t metres, find the velocity and the acceleration at t = 2 seconds.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate once to get velocity.
Put in t = 2.
Differentiate again to get acceleration.

lead.text: Same first move: one derivative of position, then put in the time.

reveal.text: You differentiated position, then substituted the time. The slope of the position graph at that instant is the velocity, not the distance travelled.

steps.headline: For s(t) = t³ metres, find the acceleration at t = 1 second.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate once to get velocity.
Differentiate again, then put in t = 1.

steps.headline: Velocity has a sign. Speed is its size.

lead.text: Positive velocity means moving in the positive direction. Negative means moving the other way.
Speed ignores direction. It is how fast, however you are going.
Watch the sign of the slope on the position graph. A falling graph is motion in the negative direction.

reveal.text: The slope was negative, so the velocity was negative. The object was moving backwards even while its position was positive.

lead.text: For s(t) = t² metres, the average velocity from 1 s to 3 s is 4 m/s. An average is not the velocity at one instant.

reveal.text: The velocity at 3 s is not the average: the object is still speeding up, so it is faster at the end than the average over the interval.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate position for velocity and velocity for acceleration, with units.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A lift is 10 m above the ground at 2 seconds and 16 m at 5 seconds. It rises steadily.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read velocity and acceleration from a position formula, and tell velocity from speed.
intro.whyItMatters: Every moving thing, from a ball to a train, is described by position, velocity and acceleration.

recap.keyIdea: Differentiate position for velocity, and again for acceleration. Velocity has a sign; speed is its size.

blocks.text: You found a velocity of 11 m/s at 2 s for 3t² − t, and an acceleration of 6 m/s². You also read −4 m/s as backwards motion.

recap.nextHook: Where the velocity is zero, the curve turns. Next: finding where.

lessons.title: Where does the curve turn?

steps.headline: Where a curve turns, its tangent is flat and the slope is zero.

lead.text: The ball's slope was positive while it rose and negative while it fell. A point with slope 0 is a stationary point.
Rising then falling is a local maximum. Falling then rising is a local minimum.

steps.headline: Find the local maximum of f(x) = 12x − x².

workedSteps.text: Differentiate.
Set the slope to zero and solve.
Check either side: the slope is positive before 6 and negative after.
Find the height at x = 6.

lead.text: Same first two moves: differentiate, then set the slope to zero.

reveal.text: You set the slope to zero and solved. That gives the x value of the candidate turning point.

steps.headline: Find the height of f(x) = 6x − x² at its peak, x = 3.

workedSteps.text: Put x = 3 into each term.
Calculate.

steps.headline: A zero slope is not enough. Check the slope on both sides.

lead.text: Positive then negative: a maximum. Negative then positive: a minimum. The same sign on both sides: no turn at all, just a flat moment.

steps.headline: On an interval, compare the ends with the stationary points.

lead.text: The highest value on [a, b] is the largest of f at each end and at each stationary point inside. The lowest is the smallest of the same values.
The graph of x² has one stationary point, at 0. The interval is [−1, 2]. Compare the ends with it.

reveal.text: The stationary point is the lowest point here, and the highest is at an end. Checking only where the slope is zero would have missed it.

lessons.orientation: Use slope signs to identify local extrema and check endpoints for an absolute maximum.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A ball's height in metres each second, from 0 s: 0, 9, 16, 21, 24, 25, 24, 21.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find where a curve turns, tell a peak from a flat spot, and find the highest value on an interval.
intro.whyItMatters: Finding the best value, the highest or the lowest, is what turning points are for.

recap.keyIdea: A curve can turn only where its slope is zero. Check the slope either side, and on an interval compare the ends too.

blocks.text: You found the peak of 12x − x² at x = 6, with height 36. You also saw that x³ is flat at 0 without turning.

recap.nextHook: Derivatives go one way. What if you only know the rate, and want the amount?

lessons.title: Undo a rate of change

steps.headline: An antiderivative undoes a derivative, and it comes with an unknown constant.

lead.text: Differentiating 3x² gives 6x. So does 3x² + 4, and 3x² − 9: a constant vanishes.
Every antiderivative of 6x is 3x² + C for some constant C. The whole family is the indefinite integral of 6x.

steps.headline: To undo xⁿ, add one to the power and divide by the new power.

lead.text: The power rule brings the power down and takes one off. Undo both moves, in reverse order.
This works for any power except n = −1.

steps.headline: F′(x) = 12x² and F(0) = 1. Find F(1).

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate: add one to the power, divide by it.
Use F(0) = 1 to fix C.
Put in x = 1.

lead.text: A whole family of functions share the same derivative. One known value picks out which of them you want.

reveal.text: You put the known value into the family and solved for C. That one number picks a single graph out of all the shifted copies.

steps.headline: F′(x) = 3x² and F(0) = 0. Find F(2).

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate.
Use F(0) = 0 to fix C.
Put in x = 2.

lead.text: The rate has two terms this time. Undo each, fix the constant, then evaluate. You can check by differentiating your answer.

reveal.text: Differentiating x³ + 2x + 1 gives back 3x² + 2, so the answer checks. Undoing a derivative can always be tested by differentiating.

lessons.orientation: Recover a family of antiderivatives and use an initial value to fix the constant.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A car moves at a steady 4 m/s. At time 0 it is 10 m from the start line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll recover a function from its rate and use a known value to pin down the constant.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing how fast something changes and where it started tells you where it is.

recap.keyIdea: Undoing a derivative gives a family F(x) + C; one known value fixes C and picks out the function.

blocks.text: You worked out that the car is 22 m from the line after 3 seconds, and that F(1) = 5 when F′(x) = 12x² and F(0) = 1.

recap.nextHook: Undoing rates can be seen as areas. Build an area from thin strips.

lessons.title: Build an area from strips

steps.headline: A rectangle adds width × height. A rate and a time make an amount.

lead.text: Your tap was two rectangles: width in minutes, height in litres per minute, area in litres.
When a rate changes smoothly, use thin strips and sample the rate at one edge of each. A left-endpoint rectangle uses the strip's left edge.

steps.headline: Use three left-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 3].

workedSteps.text: Width: the interval length over the number of strips.
Left edges are 0, 1 and 2, so the heights are 0, 1 and 2.
Add width × height for each strip.

lead.text: Split [0, 4] into two equal strips. Take each height at the left edge, then add width × height.

reveal.text: You took the height at each left edge and added the two strips. That is a left-endpoint sum.

steps.headline: Use four right-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 4].

workedSteps.text: Width: 4 over 4 strips.
Right edges are 1, 2, 3 and 4, so those are the heights.
Add width × height for each strip.

steps.headline: Left and right sums bracket the area, and thinner strips squeeze the gap.

lead.text: For an increasing curve, left rectangles sit under it and right rectangles poke above it. The exact area lies between them.
With more, narrower strips the two sums close in on the definite integral.
A midpoint rectangle takes its height at the strip's centre. On a straight line, what it leaves out and what it adds balance.

reveal.text: Centre heights 1 and 3 times width 2 gave the exact area of the triangle. For a straight line the midpoint sum has no error.

lessons.orientation: Approximate an integral with equal-width rectangles and compare sampling choices.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A tank fills at 2 litres per minute for 3 minutes. Then the rate rises to 4 litres per minute for 2 minutes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate an accumulated total with rectangle sums, and say how the estimate closes in on the integral.
intro.whyItMatters: Any amount built from a changing rate, such as water, distance or cost, is an area under a graph.

recap.keyIdea: Add width × height strip by strip. Thinner strips squeeze the sum towards the definite integral.

blocks.text: You found 14 litres by adding two rectangles, then used left, right and midpoint sums for f(x) = x. The midpoint sum of 8 was exact.

recap.nextHook: Some areas lie below the axis. What do they add?

lessons.title: When areas cancel

steps.headline: A region below the axis counts as negative in a definite integral.

lead.text: In the bath, filling added litres and draining took them away. On a rate graph, draining sits below the axis.
The definite integral adds regions above the axis and subtracts regions below it. That is signed area.
A constant rate below the axis: signed height times width.

reveal.text: The rate was negative, so the region counted as negative. The geometric area would be 6, but the signed integral is −6.

steps.headline: Find the signed integral of f(x) = x from −3 to 1.

workedSteps.text: The graph crosses the axis at x = 0, so split there.
Left triangle: base 3, height 3, below the axis.
Right triangle: base 1, height 1, above the axis.
Add the signed pieces.

steps.headline: Find the signed integral of f(x) = x from −2 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Left triangle: base 2, height 2, below the axis.
Right triangle: base 2, height 2, above the axis.
Add the signed pieces.

steps.headline: Total area adds the sizes of the pieces and ignores signs.

lead.text: Geometric area is never negative. To find it, work out each region's size separately and add them. Cancelling belongs to the signed integral.

steps.headline: Swapping the bounds flips the sign of the integral.

lead.text: The integral from b to a is the negative of the integral from a to b. The graph is the same; the direction of travel is not.
The same curve, travelled the other way: from 3 back to 1.

reveal.text: Running the interval backwards flipped the sign and left the size unchanged.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish signed accumulation from geometric area and reverse integral bounds correctly.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bath fills at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes. Then the plug is pulled, and it drains at 2 litres per minute for 3 minutes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a signed integral, say why regions can cancel, and tell it from total area.
intro.whyItMatters: Net change, such as profit or displacement, is a signed integral.

recap.keyIdea: A definite integral counts regions above the axis as positive and below as negative. Total area adds the sizes.

blocks.text: You found a net gain of 6 litres in the bath, and a signed integral of −4 for x on [−3, 1]. You also saw that x on [−2, 2] cancels to 0.

recap.nextHook: Rates and areas look like two ideas. They are one.

lessons.title: Rates and areas connect

steps.headline: The integral of a rate is the antiderivative at the top minus at the bottom.

lead.text: The triangle gave 9. The antiderivative x² has the value 9 at x = 3 and 0 at x = 0.
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 4x + 3 from 1 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate to find F.
Evaluate at the top and at the bottom.
Subtract: top minus bottom.

lead.text: Same plan: find an antiderivative, evaluate at the top and the bottom, subtract.

reveal.text: You subtracted the antiderivative's value at 1 from its value at 3. The rate was never evaluated at the ends.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 2x + 1 from 0 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Undo each term of the rate.
Evaluate at the top and bottom, then subtract.

steps.headline: Any antiderivative works, because the constant cancels.

lead.text: Take F + C. Then F(b) + C minus F(a) + C leaves F(b) − F(a). The constant appears twice and drops out, so a definite integral is one number.

steps.headline: The accumulated amount grows at exactly the current rate.

lead.text: Let A(x) be the amount accumulated from a fixed start to x. Then A′(x) = f(x): its growth rate is the rate at the moving end.
A(x) is the integral of t² + 1 from 0 to x. You do not need to integrate; ask how fast it is growing.

reveal.text: A′(x) was the rate itself, evaluated at the moving end. Integrating and differentiating undo each other.

lessons.orientation: Evaluate definite integrals with antiderivatives and differentiate accumulation functions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A graph shows the rate r(x) = 2x. It is a straight line through the origin.

intro.promise: By the end you'll evaluate a definite integral from an antiderivative, and say how fast an accumulation grows.
intro.whyItMatters: It turns every area problem into a subtraction.

recap.keyIdea: The integral of f from a to b is F(b) − F(a), and the amount accumulated grows at exactly the rate f.

blocks.text: You found the triangle's area, 9, and then reached it again as x² at 3 minus x² at 0. You also got 9 for the integral of 4x + 3 from 1 to 2.

recap.nextHook: Now put it to work: from a rate to an amount.

lessons.title: How much has changed?

To get the amount in the tank, add the starting amount. The units multiply too: L/min × min is L.

steps.headline: Inflow is 4t + 1 litres per minute. How many litres enter from t = 0 to t = 3?

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate.
Evaluate at the top and the bottom.
Subtract, top minus bottom.

lead.text: Same plan: undo the rate, evaluate at both ends, subtract.

reveal.text: You integrated the inflow over the interval and got a number of litres. That is the change, not a rate.

steps.headline: A tank starts with 7 L. Its net rate is 2t + 3 L/min. How much is in it at t = 2?

workedSteps.text: The change is the integral of the net rate.
Add the starting amount.

steps.headline: Integrate velocity for displacement, and speed for distance.

lead.text: Velocity has a sign, so forward and backward parts cancel in the integral. Speed has no sign, so its integral adds every part.

steps.headline: Net rate is the rate in minus the rate out.

lead.text: When water flows in and out at once, integrate the difference. The net rate decides whether the amount rises or falls.
Inflow is 3t + 4 L/min and outflow is a steady 2 L/min. Find the net change over the first two minutes.

reveal.text: You subtracted the rates first, then integrated the net rate. The change in the amount is the integral of the net rate.

lessons.orientation: Recover amounts from net rates while keeping track of starting values and direction.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

intro.whyItMatters: Water, money and distance are all amounts built from rates.

recap.keyIdea: Integrating a rate over an interval gives the change in the amount. Add the starting amount for the final amount.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x + 3, what value does f(x) approach as x approaches 2?
hints: Use inputs close to the stated point from both sides.
This line is continuous at the target input.
Insert the target input into x + 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nearby outputs approach 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Outputs from both sides meet at 5, and that meeting point is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is where the input is heading. The question asks where the output goes.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.
hints: Factor the difference of squares before considering the limit.
Write the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3).
Cancel the common factor for allowed nearby inputs, then approach the excluded input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Factor the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3). Away from 3 the quotient equals x + 3, which approaches 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Factor, cancel x − 3 for nearby x, then let x approach 3: 3 + 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 0/0 is not a value. Factor the top and cancel before letting x approach 3.
Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3) first, then cancel.

questions.prompt: The graph has f(x) = x + 1 for x ≠ 2, but f(2) = 5. Which statement is true?
hints: Follow the neighbouring points, not the isolated assigned value.

acceptedIdeas: The limit at 2 is 3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The surrounding line approaches 3. Changing one point to 5 does not change the limit.

choices.label: The limit at 2 is 3
The limit at 2 is 5
The limit cannot exist

questions.onCorrect: The limit is 3. The line around x = 2 decides it; the value at 2 does not.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the value assigned at x = 2. The limit follows the neighbouring points instead.
One odd point does not stop the line around it from heading somewhere.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 16)/(x − 4) as x approaches 4.
hints: Retain the excluded input when cancelling the common factor.
Write the numerator as (x − 4)(x + 4).
Approach the excluded input in the remaining linear expression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: For x ≠ 4 the quotient is x + 4, so its limit is 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Cancel the factor that causes the 0/0, then let x approach 4: 4 + 4.

misconceptions.feedback: 0/0 is not a value. Cancel the common factor first.
4 is where x is heading. Put 4 into what is left after cancelling.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 25)/(x − 5) as x approaches 5.
hints: Recognise a difference of squares.
Factor the numerator as (x − 5)(x + 5).
Use the simplified line only for the nearby inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The nearby expression is x + 5, which approaches 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Cancel x − 5, then let x approach 5: 5 + 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting x = 5 straight in gives 0/0. Cancel the common factor first.
5 is where x is heading. Put it into the cancelled expression, x + 5.

questions.prompt: Direct substitution in a quotient gives 0/0. What should happen next?
hints: Both numerator and denominator approaching zero does not determine their ratio.

acceptedIdeas: Investigate the nearby expression
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The form 0/0 is indeterminate. Simplification or another valid method is needed.

choices.label: Investigate the nearby expression
Record zero as the limit
Record one as the limit

questions.onCorrect: 0/0 settles nothing. Look at what the quotient does near the point, for instance by cancelling.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero on top does not make the whole quotient zero when the bottom is zero too.
A number over itself is 1 only when it is not zero. This one is 0/0.

questions.prompt: A function equals 2 for x < 0 and 5 for x ≥ 0. What is its left-hand limit at 0?
hints: Approach using only inputs smaller than the target.
Use the branch whose condition is x < 0.
Read the level on that branch as you move toward the boundary.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Inputs below 0 stay on the horizontal level 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Coming from the left, the graph stays on the level 2, whatever happens at 0 itself.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the level on the other side. The left-hand limit uses only inputs below 0.

questions.prompt: For that same function, what is its right-hand limit at 0?
hints: Approach using only inputs greater than the target.
Use the branch whose condition is x ≥ 0.
Read the level followed by inputs just above the boundary.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Inputs above 0 stay on the horizontal level 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. From the right, the graph stays on the level 5. The two sides head for different numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is the level on the left. The right-hand limit uses only inputs above 0.

questions.prompt: Near x = 1, f(x) = x + 2, but f(1) = 5. Is the function continuous at 1?
hints: Check all three continuity conditions.

acceptedIdeas: No: the assigned value differs from the limit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both sides approach 3, while the value is 5. Continuity requires equality too.

choices.label: No: the assigned value differs from the limit
Yes: both sides have a limit
Yes: it is defined at the point

questions.onCorrect: No. Both sides head for 3 but f(1) is 5. Continuity needs the limit to equal the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sides having a limit is only one condition. The value at the point has to match it.
Being defined is only one condition. The value also has to equal the limit.

questions.prompt: For x ≠ 2, f(x) = 2x + 4. What value must be assigned to f(2) for continuity?
hints: Use the value approached by the surrounding line.
Continuity requires the assigned value to equal the surrounding limit.
Substitute the excluded input into the surrounding linear expression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two-sided limit is 2 × 2 + 4 = 8. Assign that value at the hole.

questions.onCorrect: 8. The gap is repaired by the number the neighbours head for: 2 × 2 + 4.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 is the constant in the line. Put x = 2 into 2x + 4 to find where it is heading.
Zero is not where the line is heading. Put x = 2 into 2x + 4.

questions.prompt: For x ≠ −1, g(x) = 3x + 7. Which numerical value at −1 makes g continuous?
hints: Match the value at the point to the nearby limit.
The surrounding linear function has a well-defined limit.
Evaluate that linear expression at the excluded input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The surrounding line approaches 3(−1) + 7 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The surrounding line heads for 3 × (−1) + 7, and the gap takes that value.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is where the line crosses x = 0. Put x = −1 into 3x + 7.
Check the sign: 3 × (−1) is −3, not 3.

questions.prompt: A function's left-hand limit is 3 and its right-hand limit is 7. What is its two-sided limit?
hints: A two-sided limit must match both one-sided limits.

acceptedIdeas: It does not exist
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sides disagree, so no single number describes approach from both sides.

choices.label: It does not exist
It equals their average
It equals the right-hand limit

questions.onCorrect: No single number: the sides disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Never average them.

misconceptions.feedback: An average is not a value the function approaches from either side. The sides must agree.
Matching one side is not enough. Both sides have to head for the same number.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 1 to x = 3.
hints: Divide the output change by the input change.
Compute both endpoint heights by squaring.
Subtract those heights and divide by the difference between the inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope is (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Change in height over change in input: the slope of the secant joining the two points.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the change in height. Divide by the change in input as well.

questions.prompt: At x = 2, the secant slope for f(x) = x² is 4 + h. What does it approach as h approaches 0?
hints: Let the nonzero interval become arbitrarily small.
The formula separates a constant part and a shrinking part.
Remove the term that tends to zero and retain the constant part.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The extra h tends to zero, leaving slope 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The extra h shrinks to zero and the constant part is what the slopes head for.

misconceptions.feedback: The h term tends to 0, but the constant part stays.

questions.prompt: How is a derivative at a point obtained from secant slopes?
hints: A height and a rate of change describe different things.

acceptedIdeas: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative is the limiting slope, provided the limit exists.

choices.label: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
Substitute zero into the unsimplified denominator
Use the height of the graph

questions.onCorrect: Take the limit of the secant slopes. The limit avoids dividing by zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting h = 0 into the unsimplified quotient divides by zero. A limit gets round that.
A height and a rate are different things. The derivative is a slope.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x. Find the instantaneous rate at x = 3.
hints: Use the rate function, not the original height function.
The derivative formula already describes the instantaneous rate.
Evaluate that formula at the requested input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Evaluate the derivative: 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Evaluate the rate formula at the point: 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is the input. Put it into the rate formula 2x.
9 is the height f(3). The question asks for the rate.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 2 to x = 5.
hints: Use the two endpoint values.
Square each endpoint to find its height.
Divide the difference of heights by the difference of inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output change is 25 − 4 = 21 over input change 3, so the rate is 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Change in height, 25 − 4, over change in input, 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 21 is the change in height. Divide by the change in input as well.

questions.prompt: A function has f(2) = 9 and f′(2) = −3. Which statement describes its instantaneous rate?
hints: Distinguish the function value from its derivative.

acceptedIdeas: It is falling at 3 output units per input unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative −3 gives the signed local rate; 9 is the height.

choices.label: It is falling at 3 output units per input unit
Its height is negative three
It is rising at nine units per input unit

questions.onCorrect: f′(2) = −3 is a rate with a sign: negative means falling, 3 units per input unit.

misconceptions.feedback: −3 is the derivative, not the height. The height is f(2).
9 is the height, not the rate. The sign of the derivative also matters.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³, find f′(2).
hints: Differentiate the power before substituting.
For x cubed the derivative is three times x squared.
Square the requested input, then multiply by the derivative coefficient.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The derivative is 3x²; at 2 it is 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Bring the power down, drop it by one, then substitute: 3 × 2².

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the height, 2³. You need the slope, so differentiate first.
That is 3 × 2. After bringing the 3 down the power drops to 2; then substitute.

questions.prompt: For g(x) = 2x² + 5, find g′(1).
hints: A vertical shift does not change a slope.
The derivative of the squared term is linear; the constant drops out.
Evaluate that linear derivative at the requested input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The derivative is 4x because the constant contributes zero; at 1 it is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The constant 5 only lifts the graph. Differentiate 2x² to get 4x.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is the height g(1). The question asks for the slope.
The 5 shifts the graph but does not change its slope.

questions.prompt: Which expression is the derivative of 3x² − 2x + 7?
hints: The constant term contributes no rate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Differentiate each term: 6x, −2 and zero.

questions.onCorrect: 6x − 2. Differentiate term by term; the constant gives nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: The constant 7 gives zero slope, so it should not appear.
The 3x² term needs the power rule: 3 × 2 is 6, not 3.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = 4 − x², find f′(1).
hints: Retain the negative coefficient.
Differentiate the squared term while retaining its coefficient.
Substitute the input into the resulting linear derivative.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Differentiating gives −2x, so the slope at 1 is −2.

questions.onCorrect: −2. Differentiate to get −2x; at 1 the slope is negative, so the graph is falling.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. The x² term has coefficient −1.
3 is the height f(1). The question asks for the slope.

questions.prompt: For p(x) = 2x³ − 5x + 9, find p′(2).
hints: The linear term becomes its coefficient.
Differentiate the cubic and linear terms separately.
Evaluate both derivative terms at the requested input and combine them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: p′(x) = 6x² − 5; at 2 this is 24 − 5 = 19.

questions.onCorrect: 19. Differentiate each term: 6x² − 5, then substitute 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 is the cubic term's slope only. Differentiate the −5x term as well.
Check the sign: the −5x term gives −5, not +5.
15 is the height p(2). The question asks for the slope.

questions.prompt: Adding 10 to a differentiable function changes its derivative in which way?
hints: Compare differences before and after the shift.

acceptedIdeas: It leaves the derivative unchanged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A vertical translation leaves all output differences unchanged.

choices.label: It leaves the derivative unchanged
It adds ten to every slope
It multiplies every slope by ten

questions.onCorrect: Unchanged. Adding a constant lifts the graph but leaves every slope alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding ten shifts the graph vertically. It does not make it steeper.
Multiplying the slopes would need multiplying the function, not adding to it.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = (2x + 1)², find f′(1).
hints: Multiply the outer rate by the inner rate.
The derivative is the outer square's rate multiplied by the slope of the inner line.
Evaluate the inner expression, then multiply by both rate factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain rule gives 2(2x + 1) × 2. At 1 the result is 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Outer rate 2(2x + 1) = 6 at x = 1, times the inner rate 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the outer rate only. Multiply by how fast the inside changes as well.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = (3 − x)², find f′(1).
hints: The inner expression decreases as x increases.
The derivative of the inner expression is negative.
Multiply twice the inner expression by its signed rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The derivative is 2(3 − x) × (−1); at 1 it equals −4.

questions.onCorrect: −4. The outer rate is 4, and the inside falls as x grows, so multiply by −1.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the inner rate: 3 − x falls as x grows, so it is negative.

questions.prompt: Which is the derivative of (3x + 1)²?
hints: Count both stages of the change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative of the square is evaluated at 3x + 1, then multiplied by the inner derivative 3.

questions.onCorrect: 6(3x + 1). Twice the inner value, times the inner rate 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 2(3x + 1) is only the outer rate. Multiply by how fast 3x + 1 changes.
The inner expression stays inside the bracket. 3x + 1 is not differentiated on its own.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = (x + 2)³, find f′(1).
hints: The inner rate is one.
The derivative of a cube is three times the square of its input.
Square the inner value before multiplying by both rate factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 3(x + 2)²; at 1 this gives 27.

questions.onCorrect: 27. Outer rate 3(x + 2)² at x = 1, times the inner rate 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Square the inner value, 3, then multiply by the power.
3 is the power. The outer rate is 3 times the square of the inner value.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = (2x − 1)³, find f′(2).
hints: There is an inner factor as well as the cubic power.
The outer rate is three times the square of the inner expression.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner line after evaluating its squared value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 6(2x − 1)²; at 2 the rate is 6 × 9 = 54.

questions.onCorrect: 54. Outer rate 3(2x − 1)² = 27, times the inner rate 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 is the outer rate only. Multiply by the inner rate, 2.
18 is 2 × 9. The outer rate has a 3 in front of the squared inner value.

questions.prompt: Why is differentiating only the outer function insufficient for a composition?
hints: Follow the change through both functions.

acceptedIdeas: The inner input may change at a different rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The chain rule accounts for how rapidly the inner input changes with x.

choices.label: The inner input may change at a different rate
Every composition has a constant slope
The outer derivative must be added to the original function

questions.onCorrect: The inside has its own rate. The chain rule multiplies the outer rate by it.

misconceptions.feedback: A composition's slope is not constant. The outer rate depends on the inner value.
Rates in a chain multiply. Nothing is added to the original function.

questions.prompt: Position is s(t) = t² + 2t metres. Find velocity at t = 2 seconds in m/s.
hints: Take one derivative of position.
Differentiate each position term with respect to time.
Substitute the requested time into the velocity expression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Velocity is 2t + 2, so at 2 seconds it is 6 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Velocity is the derivative of position: 2t + 2, which is 6 at t = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 m is the position s(2). Velocity is the derivative.
The 2t term differentiates to 2. Check each term of the position.

questions.prompt: Position is s(t) = t³ metres. Find acceleration at t = 1 second in m/s².
hints: Acceleration is the second derivative of position.
Differentiate the cubic once to obtain velocity.
Differentiate that velocity again before evaluating the time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Velocity is 3t² and acceleration is 6t, giving 6 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s². Acceleration is the second derivative: 3t² gives 6t, which is 6 at t = 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is the velocity at t = 1. Differentiate once more for acceleration.
1 m is the position s(1). Differentiate twice.

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity −2 m/s. What is its speed?
hints: A magnitude is nonnegative.

acceptedIdeas: 2 m/s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so it is 2 m/s.

choices.label: 2 m/s
Negative two metres per second
Zero metres per second

questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. Speed is the size of velocity; the minus sign only gives direction.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed has no direction, so it cannot be negative.
Zero would mean standing still. This particle is moving, just in the negative direction.

questions.prompt: For s(t) = t² metres, find instantaneous velocity at t = 3 seconds in m/s.
hints: Use a derivative at the instant, not an average over an interval.
The derivative of the squared time is linear in time.
Evaluate this instantaneous rate at the requested time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: s′(t) = 2t, so the velocity is 6 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. The derivative 2t at t = 3 is the velocity at that instant, not an average.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 m/s is the average over 1 s to 3 s. The question asks about one instant.
9 m is the position s(3). Velocity is the derivative.

questions.prompt: Position is s(t) = 2t³ − 3t² metres. Find acceleration at t = 2 seconds in m/s².
hints: Differentiate twice and then substitute the time.
The velocity is quadratic minus a linear term.
Differentiate both velocity terms and substitute the requested time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Velocity is 6t² − 6t; acceleration is 12t − 6, giving 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18 m/s². Differentiate twice: 6t² − 6t, then 12t − 6, then put in t = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 m/s is the velocity at t = 2. Differentiate once more for acceleration.
4 m is the position s(2). Differentiate twice.

questions.prompt: What units does the second derivative of position in metres with respect to time in seconds have?
hints: Track the units through both derivatives.

acceptedIdeas: Metres per second squared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each derivative divides the units by seconds once more.

choices.label: Metres per second squared
Metres per second
Square metres

questions.onCorrect: Metres per second squared. Each derivative divides the units by seconds once more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the unit of velocity. Acceleration divides by seconds once more.
Derivatives divide by time. They do not square the metres.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = 6x − x², at which x is f′(x) zero?
hints: Differentiate and solve for a zero slope.
The derivative is a constant minus a linear term.
Set that expression equal to zero and isolate the input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Solve 6 − 2x = 0 to obtain x = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Differentiate, set the slope to zero, and solve: 6 − 2x = 0.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the constant in the slope formula. Set 6 − 2x equal to zero and solve.
9 is the height of the curve, not where the slope is zero.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = 6x − x², what is the height at its local maximum x = 3?
hints: Evaluate the original function at the turning point.
The requested quantity is height, not the input coordinate.
Substitute the given peak input into the original quadratic.
questions.onCorrect: 9. The turning point is at x = 3. Its height comes from the original function: 18 − 9.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is where the peak is. The question asks for its height.
18 is 6 × 3 only. Take away the x² term as well.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³, the derivative at 0 is zero. What happens there?
hints: Inspect neighbouring slopes, not just the zero slope.

acceptedIdeas: The curve keeps increasing through a flat point
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The slope is positive on both sides of 0, so there is no turn.

choices.label: The curve keeps increasing through a flat point
The curve reaches a local maximum
The curve reaches a local minimum

questions.onCorrect: The slope is positive on both sides of 0, so the curve keeps rising through the flat point.

misconceptions.feedback: A maximum needs the slope to change from positive to negative. Check the slope either side of 0.
A minimum needs the slope to change from negative to positive. Check the slope either side of 0.

questions.prompt: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x² on [−1, 2].
hints: Check endpoints as well as the interior stationary point.
Compare both endpoint heights with the interior critical point's height.
The squared function's stationary point is a minimum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Compare f(−1) = 1, f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 4. The maximum is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Compare the ends and the stationary point: the largest value is at the right end.

misconceptions.feedback: 0 is the height at the stationary point, which is a minimum here. Compare the ends too.
1 is the left end's height. Check the right end as well.

questions.prompt: Find the maximum value of f(x) = 8x − x² on [0, 6].
hints: Find the stationary point, then compare all candidate values.
Solve for the zero of the derivative, keeping only points in the interval.
Evaluate the original function at that point and both endpoints; select the largest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The interior critical point is x = 4, giving 16. Endpoint values are 0 and 12.

questions.onCorrect: 16. The stationary point x = 4 gives 16, higher than either end.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the right end's height. The stationary point gives a higher value.
4 is where the stationary point is. The question asks for the height.

questions.prompt: For a differentiable function, why is f′(a) = 0 alone insufficient to prove a local extremum?
hints: Use neighbouring behaviour to classify a candidate.

acceptedIdeas: The function may keep increasing through a
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A flat tangent can occur without a direction change, as for a cubic at zero.

choices.label: The function may keep increasing through a
The derivative must equal the function value
A horizontal tangent always marks a discontinuity

questions.onCorrect: A zero slope can occur without a turn, as for x³. Check the slope on both sides.

misconceptions.feedback: The derivative and the function value are different things. They need not be equal.
A horizontal tangent is a smooth point. The curve may even keep rising through it.

questions.prompt: An antiderivative of 2x has the form x² + C. If F(0) = 3, what is C?
hints: Substitute the initial input into the proposed antiderivative.
Substitute zero into x squared plus the constant.
Match the remaining constant to the supplied initial value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At zero, x² + C equals C, so C = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. At x = 0, x² vanishes and only C is left, so C matches F(0).

misconceptions.feedback: x² is 0 at x = 0, so what is left must match F(0).

questions.prompt: Let F′(x) = 3x² and F(0) = 0. Find F(2).
hints: Raise the exponent and divide by the new exponent.
The antiderivative of the given rate is a cubic plus a constant.
Use the zero initial value to fix the constant, then evaluate the cubic.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The antiderivative is x³ + C. The initial value gives C = 0, so F(2) = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Undo 3x² to get x³, fix C with F(0) = 0, then put in x = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the rate F′(2). You need the function F.
6 is 3 × 2. To undo the derivative, add one to the power and divide by it.

questions.prompt: Which describes all antiderivatives of 2x on the real line?
hints: A derivative cannot reveal a vertical shift.

acceptedIdeas: x² + C, where C is any constant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every vertical shift of x² has derivative 2x.

choices.label: x² + C, where C is any constant
Only x²
2x + C

questions.onCorrect: x² + C. Every vertical shift of x² has derivative 2x.

misconceptions.feedback: Shifting x² up or down does not change its derivative, so it is not the only one.
2x is the derivative itself, not an antiderivative.

questions.prompt: Let F′(x) = 3x² + 2 and F(0) = 1. Find F(2).
hints: Integrate each term and then use the initial value.
The antiderivative is a cubic plus a linear term and a constant.
Use the initial value to fix the constant before evaluating the requested input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It rose 16 − 10 = 6 m in 5 − 2 = 3 s, so 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Change in height over change in time: a rate of change of position.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 m is the height gained. Divide by the time it took.
3 s is the time taken. The question asks for a rate.

questions.prompt: Why is the acceleration the same number at every time?
hints: Acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph. What does that graph look like?

acceptedIdeas: Velocity 6t − 1 is a straight line, so its slope never changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Velocity 6t − 1 is a straight line in t, so its slope is the same everywhere.

choices.label: Velocity 6t − 1 is a straight line, so its slope never changes
The position never changes
Acceleration is the same in every motion

questions.onCorrect: Acceleration is the slope of velocity. A straight-line velocity has one slope throughout.

misconceptions.feedback: The position changes all the time. It is the velocity's slope that is constant.
Many motions speed up and slow down by different amounts. This one is special.

questions.prompt: A position is s(t) = t² − 6t metres. What is the velocity at t = 1 second, in m/s?
hints: Differentiate each term of the position.
v(t) = 2t − 6. Put in t = 1.
2 × 1 is 2. Take 6 away.
questions.onCorrect: −4. The sign says the object is moving in the negative direction.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: at t = 1 the position is falling, so the velocity is negative.
−5 m is the position s(1). The question asks for the velocity.

questions.prompt: A position is s(t) = 5t² metres. What is the velocity at t = 2 seconds, in m/s?
hints: Differentiate the position once.
5t² gives 5 × 2t.
Put t = 2 into 10t.
questions.onCorrect: 20. Velocity is one derivative of position: 10t.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 m/s² is the acceleration. Velocity comes from one derivative.
Check the arithmetic: multiply the coefficient by the time.

questions.prompt: A position is s(t) = t² − 10t metres. What is the velocity at t = 2 seconds, in m/s?
hints: Differentiate each term of the position.
v(t) = 2t − 10. Put in t = 2.
2 × 2 is 4. Take 10 away.
questions.onCorrect: −6. A negative velocity means moving backwards.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: at t = 2 the position is falling.
−16 m is the position s(2). Velocity is the derivative.

questions.prompt: How much water goes into the tank in total, in litres?
hints: How many litres arrive during the first 3 minutes?
The first stretch gives 6 L. What about the last 2 minutes?
Add the two amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 × 2 = 6 L in the first stretch and 2 × 4 = 8 L in the second: 14 L.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Each stretch is rate × time, and the stretches add.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 L is only the first stretch. The rate changes, so the tank keeps filling.
Each rate lasts a different time. Multiply each rate by its time before adding.

questions.prompt: Why are the left-endpoint heights 0, 1 and 2, and not 1, 2 and 3?
hints: Where on each strip is the height taken?

acceptedIdeas: Each strip uses its left edge: 0, 1 and 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A left-endpoint rectangle takes its height at the left edge of its strip, so the edges are 0, 1 and 2.

choices.label: Each strip uses its left edge: 0, 1 and 2
The function is zero at the end
The heights always start at 1

questions.onCorrect: Each strip uses the function at its left edge, so the heights are 0, 1 and 2.

misconceptions.feedback: The strips are what matter. Look at where each one starts.
The first strip starts at 0, so its left edge is 0.

questions.prompt: Use three equal-width left-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x² on [0, 6]. Find their sum.
hints: What is the width of each strip?
The width is 2. Where are the left edges? Square each.
Add the squared heights, then multiply by the width.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The width is 2 and the left heights are 0², 2² and 4², so the sum is 2 × (0 + 4 + 16) = 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. Width times the sum of the left-edge heights.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the heights. Multiply by the width as well.
That uses right edges. A left-endpoint sum uses the left edge of each strip.

questions.prompt: A strip is 0.5 wide and 6 tall. What area does it add?
hints: What do you multiply to get a rectangle's area?
Width times height.
What is 0.5 × 6?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Area is width × height: 0.5 × 6 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A strip's contribution is its width times its height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height. The area is width × height.
Area is a product, not a sum.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², the slope at x = 1 is 2, at x = 2 it is 4, at x = 3 it is 6 and at x = 5 it is 10. What do you expect the slope to be at x = 7?
hints: Compare each slope with its x. What is the pattern?
Each slope is double its x.
Double 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each slope is twice the x value, so at 7 it is 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Each slope is twice its x. That pattern is the derivative 2x.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is the x value. Compare each x with its slope to find the pattern.
49 is the height of the curve at 7. The pattern is about slopes.

questions.prompt: In 4x³, where does the 4 come from?
hints: Look at what the power was before you differentiated.

acceptedIdeas: The old power of x
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The old power, 4, comes down to the front as a multiplier.

choices.label: The old power of x
The number of terms
The slope at x = 1

questions.onCorrect: The power comes down as a multiplier, and the power itself drops by one.

misconceptions.feedback: There is only one term here. Compare 4x³ with the x⁴ you started from.
The 4 is part of the rate formula, before any x value is put in.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x² − 6x, at which x is f′(x) = 0?
hints: Differentiate each term first. What is f′(x)?
f′(x) = 2x − 6. Set it equal to zero.
Add 6 to both sides, then halve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 2x − 6. Setting 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Differentiate each term, then solve for where the slope is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the coefficient. Solve 2x − 6 = 0 for x.
Check the sign: 2x = 6 gives a positive x.

questions.prompt: What is the slope of f(x) = x⁵ at x = 2?
hints: Differentiate first. What does x⁵ become?
5x⁴. Now put in x = 2.
2⁴ is 16. Multiply by 5.
questions.onCorrect: 80. Bring the 5 down, drop the power to 4, then substitute 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 32 is the height 2⁵. The question asks for the slope.
That is 5 × 2. The power should drop to 4 before you substitute.

questions.prompt: What is the slope of f(x) = 5x² + 7 at x = 3?
hints: Differentiate each term. What happens to the 7?
The 5x² term gives 5 × 2x.
Put x = 3 into 10x.
questions.onCorrect: 30. The 7 vanishes; 5x² gives 10x.

misconceptions.feedback: 52 is the height f(3). The question asks for the slope.
The constant 7 has slope zero, so it does not add to the answer.

questions.prompt: What is the area under the graph of r(x) = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3?
hints: What shape is the region under a straight line from 0?
The base is 3. How tall is the line at x = 3?
Half of base times height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The region is a triangle with base 3 and height 2 × 3 = 6, so its area is ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. A triangle is half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is base × height. A triangle is half of that.
6 is the height at x = 3. The area needs the base too.

questions.prompt: Why subtract F(a) from F(b)?
hints: F(b) counts everything up to b. What does F(a) count?

acceptedIdeas: It is the total at b minus the total at a
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F(b) is the total built up to b and F(a) is the total built up to a. The difference is what was added from a to b.

choices.label: It is the total at b minus the total at a
To make the answer positive
Because a is smaller than b

questions.onCorrect: F(b) − F(a) is what accumulates between a and b: the total at the end minus the total at the start.

misconceptions.feedback: The result can be negative. The subtraction removes what built up before a.
The order is set by what accumulates, not by which number is smaller.

questions.prompt: A pool gains water at r(t) = 6t litres per minute. How many litres does it gain between t = 1 and t = 3 minutes?
hints: Which function has derivative 6t?
3t² does. Find its value at t = 3 and t = 1.
Subtract the value at 1 from the value at 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An antiderivative of 6t is 3t². Then 3 × 9 − 3 × 1 = 27 − 3 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. Undo the rate, then subtract the totals at the ends.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 is the total at t = 3 only. Subtract the total at t = 1.
18 is the rate at t = 3. The question asks for an amount.

questions.prompt: F(x) = 2x² has derivative 4x. Use it to find the integral of 4x from 0 to 3.
hints: Which function do you evaluate at the ends?
Put 3 and 0 into 2x².
Top minus bottom.
questions.onCorrect: 18. The antiderivative at the top minus the antiderivative at the bottom.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the rate at x = 3. You need the antiderivative's values at the ends.

questions.prompt: A(x) is the amount accumulated from 0 to x at rate f(t) = 3t. How fast is A growing at x = 4?
hints: How fast does an accumulation grow at a moment?
At the current rate, f.
Put 4 into f.
questions.onCorrect: 12. The accumulation grows at exactly the current rate.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 is the amount accumulated, A(4). The question asks how fast it is growing.
3 is the coefficient in the rate. Put x = 4 into the rate itself.

questions.prompt: As your basket total creeps up towards £20 from below, what delivery fee in pounds do you pay?
hints: Which fee applies to a basket of £19.99?
The £7 fee only starts at £20 and above.
Every basket just under £20 pays the same fee. Which?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every basket below £20 pays £3, so the fee heads for £3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. From below, every basket pays the lower fee, so that is where the fee heads.

misconceptions.feedback: £7 starts only at £20. Coming up from below, the basket is still under £20.
The fees are not added together. A basket pays one or the other.

questions.prompt: The limit at 2 exists and f(2) is defined. Why is f still not continuous at 2?
hints: Compare the number the neighbours head for with the number f(2) gives.

acceptedIdeas: The limit and the value are different numbers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit is 4 and the value is 7. Continuity needs them to be equal.

choices.label: The limit and the value are different numbers
A limit and a value cannot both exist
The two sides disagree

questions.onCorrect: Continuity compares the limit with the value. Here they are different numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: They can both exist. A limit ignores the value at the point, which is why they can differ.
Look back at the left and right lines: they ended at the same number.

questions.prompt: A function has left-hand limit 6 and right-hand limit 6 at x = 1, but f(1) is not defined. Which is true?
hints: Check the three conditions one at a time.

acceptedIdeas: f has a two-sided limit at 1 but is not continuous there
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sides agree, so the two-sided limit is 6. But f(1) does not exist, so it cannot equal the limit.

choices.label: f is continuous at 1
f has a two-sided limit at 1 but is not continuous there
f has no limit at 1

questions.onCorrect: The limit exists, but with no value at the point the function is not continuous there.

misconceptions.feedback: Continuity needs a value at the point. Here there is none to match the limit.
Both one-sided limits are 6, and they agree.

questions.prompt: A function gives 3 for inputs below 5 and 9 for inputs of 5 or more. What is its right-hand limit at 5?
hints: Which inputs does a right-hand limit use?
Inputs larger than 5. Which rule applies to them?
Read off what that rule gives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From above, every input gives 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. From the right, every input is 5 or more and gives 9.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is the left-hand limit. The right-hand limit uses inputs above 5.

questions.prompt: A function's left-hand limit at 2 is 4 and its right-hand limit is 4. What is its two-sided limit at 2?
hints: Do the two sides agree?
They head for the same number.
That shared number is the limit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sides agree on 4, so the two-sided limit is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. When the sides agree, that shared number is the two-sided limit.

misconceptions.feedback: The sides are not added. When they agree, the shared number is the limit.

questions.prompt: How far from the start line is it after 3 seconds, in metres?
hints: How far does it travel in 3 seconds at 4 m/s?
The travel is only part of the answer. Where did it begin?
Add the starting distance to the distance travelled.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It covers 4 × 3 = 12 m and began 10 m out, so it is 22 m from the start line.

questions.onCorrect: 22. The distance covered, plus where it began: a rate undone, plus a starting value.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 m is the distance covered. The car did not start at the line.
Add the starting distance to how far it travelled, not to the speed.

questions.prompt: Why divide by 3 when undoing 12x²?
hints: What does differentiating x³ do to the 3?

acceptedIdeas: Differentiating x³ multiplies by 3, so we divide by 3 to undo it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Differentiating x³ multiplies by 3, so undoing it means dividing by 3.

choices.label: Differentiating x³ multiplies by 3, so we divide by 3 to undo it
To make the answer smaller
Because we always divide

questions.onCorrect: Differentiating multiplies by the new power. Undoing it divides by that power.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing is part of undoing the power rule, not a way to shrink the answer.
The division undoes the multiplication that differentiating does.

questions.prompt: A tank holds 50 litres at time 0 and gains water at rate 4t litres per minute. How many litres are in it at t = 3 minutes?
hints: Which function has derivative 4t?
2t² has derivative 4t. How much is gained by t = 3?
Add the 50 litres that were already there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The amount gained is 2t², which is 18 by t = 3. With the 50 litres already there, the total is 68.

questions.onCorrect: 68. Undo the rate to get the amount gained, then add the starting amount.

misconceptions.feedback: 18 litres is what was added. The tank started with some water.
12 is the rate at t = 3, in litres per minute. The question asks for an amount.

questions.prompt: Let F′(x) = 6x² and F(0) = 0. What is F(2)?
hints: Add one to the power and divide by it. What does 6x² become?
6x³ divided by 3 is 2x³.
Put x = 2 into 2x³.
questions.onCorrect: 16. Undo 6x² to get 2x³, then put in x = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 is the rate F′(2). You need F(2).
Remember the 2 in 2x³: 2 × 8.

questions.prompt: At which second is the ball highest?
hints: Read along the list. Where do the heights stop rising?
The heights go up, then come down. Find the top.
The largest height is 25. At which second is it?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The heights rise to 25 m and then fall, so the top is at 5 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The heights stop rising and start falling there, which is where the ball turns.

misconceptions.feedback: 25 is the height. The question asks for the time.
At 6 seconds the height is 24, lower than the second before.

questions.prompt: Why does a slope that goes from positive to negative mean a maximum?
hints: What does a positive slope do to the height? A negative one?

acceptedIdeas: The curve rises and then falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Positive slope means rising and negative slope means falling, so the curve rises and then falls.

choices.label: The curve rises and then falls
The slope is zero at that point
The height there is positive

questions.onCorrect: Rising then falling is a peak, so the point between them is a local maximum.

misconceptions.feedback: That is true, but it is also true for other points. Think about what happens either side.
The height can be negative at a peak. The slopes either side are what tell you.

questions.prompt: Find the minimum value of f(x) = x² − 6x on [0, 5].
hints: Find where the slope is zero, and keep it only if it is in the interval.
Compare f at x = 0, at x = 5 and at the stationary point.
The stationary point is x = 3. Work out f(3) and compare.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 2x − 6 is zero at x = 3, where f(3) = −9. The ends give f(0) = 0 and f(5) = −5, so the minimum is −9.

questions.onCorrect: −9. The lowest of the end values and the stationary value.

misconceptions.feedback: −5 is the height at the right end. The stationary point is lower.
3 is where the minimum occurs. The question asks for its value.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x² − 8x, at which x is the slope zero?
hints: Differentiate first. What is f′(x)?
f′(x) = 2x − 8. Set it to zero.
Add 8, then halve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 2x − 8 = 0 gives x = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A stationary point is where the slope is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the coefficient. Solve 2x − 8 = 0.
−16 is the height at the turning point. The question asks for where it is.

questions.prompt: Find the highest value of f(x) = 2x + 1 on [0, 3].
hints: Is the slope ever zero?
With no stationary point, only the ends are candidates.
Compare f(0) and f(3).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope is never zero, so the highest value is at an end: f(3) = 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. With no stationary point, the maximum is at an end.

misconceptions.feedback: 1 is the lowest value, at the left end. The question asks for the highest.

flashcards.front: Find the limit of (x² − 36)/(x − 6) as x approaches 6.
flashcards.back: For x ≠ 6, simplify to x + 6; the limit is 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: For x ≠ 6, simplify to x + 6; the limit is 12.

flashcards.front: For x ≠ −3, f(x) = x + 8, while f(−3) = 20. Find the limit at −3.
flashcards.back: Nearby values approach −3 + 8 = 5, independently of the assigned value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nearby values approach −3 + 8 = 5, independently of the assigned value.

flashcards.front: A function equals −4 below x = 2 and 6 at or above 2. Find its left-hand limit at 2.
flashcards.back: Approaching from smaller inputs stays at −4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Approaching from smaller inputs stays at −4.

flashcards.front: For x ≠ 3, g(x) = 2x − 1. Which value at 3 makes g continuous?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The surrounding graph approaches 2 × 3 − 1 = 5.

flashcards.front: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 3 to x = 6.
For f(x) = x², the secant slope at x = 4 is 8 + h. Find its limit as h approaches 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The limiting slope is 8.

flashcards.front: For f(x) = 3x³ + 2x, find f′(1).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f′(x) = 9x² + 2, giving 11.

flashcards.front: For f(x) = 7 − 2x², find f′(3).
For f(x) = (4x + 1)², find f′(1).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2(4x + 1) × 4 gives 40 at x = 1.

flashcards.front: For f(x) = (5 − 2x)², find f′(1).
Position is s(t) = 3t² − 5t metres. Find velocity at t = 2 seconds in m/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: s′(t) = 6t − 5, giving 7 m/s.

flashcards.front: Position is s(t) = t³ + 4t metres. Find acceleration at t = 3 seconds in m/s².
flashcards.back: The second derivative is 6t, giving 18 m/s².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second derivative is 6t, giving 18 m/s².

flashcards.front: For f(x) = 10x − x², at which x is the derivative zero?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 − 2x = 0 gives x = 5.

flashcards.front: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x² on [−3, 1].
flashcards.back: The values at −3, 0 and 1 are 9, 0 and 1. The maximum is 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values at −3, 0 and 1 are 9, 0 and 1. The maximum is 9.

flashcards.front: Let F′(x) = 6x and F(0) = 2. Find F(2).
Let F′(x) = 2x + 5 and F(0) = −1. Find F(3).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F(x) = x² + 5x − 1, giving 23.

flashcards.front: Use three left-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 6]. Find their sum.
flashcards.back: Width is 2 and heights are 0, 2, 4. The sum is 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Width is 2 and heights are 0, 2, 4. The sum is 12.

flashcards.front: Use three midpoint rectangles for f(x) = 2x on [0, 3]. Find their sum.
flashcards.back: Width is 1 and midpoint heights are 1, 3, 5, giving 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Width is 1 and midpoint heights are 1, 3, 5, giving 9.

flashcards.front: Find the integral of the constant −3 from 1 to 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Signed height −3 times width 4 gives −12.

flashcards.front: Find the signed integral of f(x) = 2x from −1 to 2.
flashcards.back: An antiderivative is x², so the integral is 4 − 1 = 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An antiderivative is x², so the integral is 4 − 1 = 3.

flashcards.front: Evaluate the integral of 4x + 2 from 1 to 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An antiderivative is 2x² + 2x; 24 − 4 = 20.

flashcards.front: A(x) is the integral from 1 to x of (3t + 2) dt. Find A′(4).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A′(x) = 3x + 2, giving 14.

flashcards.front: A tank starts with 4 L and its net rate is t + 2 L/min. Find the amount after 2 minutes in litres.
flashcards.back: The change is [t²/2 + 2t] from 0 to 2 = 6 L. Adding 4 L gives 10 L.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is [t²/2 + 2t] from 0 to 2 = 6 L. Adding 4 L gives 10 L.

flashcards.front: Velocity is v(t) = 4t − 3 m/s. Find signed displacement from 0 to 2 seconds in metres.
flashcards.back: The integral is [2t² − 3t] from 0 to 2 = 8 − 6 = 2 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The integral is [2t² − 3t] from 0 to 2 = 8 − 6 = 2 m.

For x ≠ 3, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) equals x + 3, so its limit at 3 is 6.
Assigning a different value at the hole leaves the neighbouring values alone, so the limit can differ from f at the point.

Nearby outputs approach 2 + 3 = 5.
Factor the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3). Away from 3 the quotient equals x + 3, which approaches 6.
The surrounding line approaches 3. Changing one point to 5 does not change the limit.
